Paper_name: Expanding and Retracting From the Self: Gains and Costs in Switching Self-Associations
Summary: Two experiments examined the formation and breaking of associations between geometric shapes and personal labels (self, friend, stranger). Participants first learned shape-label associations and then had to relearn them after the pairings were switched. Results showed faster and more accurate responses when forming new associations to self-related stimuli. Conversely, there were slower reaction times and reduced accuracy when trying to break old self-associations, especially on mismatch trials involving shapes previously linked to the self. The findings suggest self-reference acts as a strong 'memorial glue,' facilitating new learning but causing interference from old associations.
Author: Haixu Wang, Glyn Humphreys, Jie Sui
Journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
Conclusion: Self-reference enhances the binding of associations in memory, which facilitates the formation of new self-related associations. However, this strong binding also creates a cost, making it difficult to switch away from old self-associations, leading to interference and slower performance when prior self-linked stimuli must be reassigned.
